cues.text: Section three covers ITIL and service management.
ITIL, which stands for Information Technology Infrastructure Library, provides guidance for managing IT-enabled services.
Let us begin with what a service actually is.
A service facilitates outcomes that customers want, without requiring those customers to manage every underlying cost and risk.
Consider a customer using mobile banking.
That customer wants reliable transfers.
They do not want to be responsible for something like database replication.
The service provider takes on that burden, and the customer receives the outcome.
Now let us look at how ITIL is structured, starting with the traditional ITIL version 3 lifecycle.
It has five stages: service strategy, service design, service transition, service operation, and continual service improvement.
Each has a distinct role.
Service strategy determines value and priorities.
Service design defines requirements.
Service transition introduces changes.
Service operation delivers and supports services.
And continual service improvement uses feedback to make things better.
ITIL 4 takes a different approach.
Instead of a linear lifecycle, it uses a service value system, abbreviated SVS.
This system includes guiding principles, governance, the service value chain, practices, and continual improvement.
The service value chain has six activities: plan, improve, engage, design and transition, obtain or build, and deliver and support.
ITIL 4 also describes four dimensions: organisations and people, information and technology, partners and suppliers, and value streams and processes.
Two further ideas are worth holding onto.
First, value is co-created with customers and other stakeholders.
It is not simply handed over by the provider.
Second, continual improvement follows a cycle.
You measure the current state, define the desired outcomes, implement improvements, and then review the results.
Finally, be careful not to confuse four closely related practices.
Incident management aims to restore service quickly.
Problem management addresses underlying causes.
Change enablement assesses and authorises changes.
And service request management fulfils routine requests.
A short example helps separate them.
A failed payment gateway is an incident, because service must be restored quickly.
A recurring connection-pool defect is a problem, because the underlying cause needs to be addressed.
Deploying a fix is a change, because it must be assessed and authorised.
And requesting access is a service request, because it is a routine request to be fulfilled.
